title: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success
author: Dr. Carol S. Dweck
summary:
Mindset distills decades of Carol Dweck's research into a single, deceptively simple idea: the belief you hold about whether ability is fixed or developable changes almost everything about how you pursue goals, handle setbacks, and relate to other people. Dweck calls these two belief systems the fixed mindset — the assumption that intelligence, talent, and character are essentially set traits you either have or don't — and the growth mindset — the assumption that those same qualities can be built through effort, strategy, and support from others. The distinction sounds abstract until Dweck shows how much downstream behavior it predicts: in her research, children and adults with a fixed mindset consistently chose easier tasks they knew they could ace, while those with a growth mindset gravitated toward harder ones that promised more to learn, even at the cost of looking less capable in the moment.

That difference in orientation cascades outward. In a fixed mindset, every challenge becomes a referendum on whether you 'have it,' so effort itself gets reinterpreted as bad news — if you needed to work hard, you probably weren't talented to begin with. Negative feedback becomes a threat to be deflected rather than information to use, and someone else's success becomes a comparison that diminishes you. In a growth mindset, the same events land differently: a hard problem is an opportunity, effort is the mechanism that builds the very ability you're trying to develop, criticism is useful data, and another person's success is evidence of what's possible rather than a verdict on your own worth.

Dweck traces this pattern across several arenas most readers will recognize from their own lives. In sports and other high-performance fields, she argues that sustained development — not raw early talent — is what actually explains most exceptional achievement, and profiles athletes and coaches who treated losses as data rather than identity threats. In business, she contrasts fixed-mindset executives who need to be visibly the smartest person in the room, and who surround themselves with people who won't challenge them, with growth-minded leaders who build organizations that keep learning and can eventually outgrow their founder. In close relationships, she shows how a fixed mindset reads conflict or a partner's flaws as proof of fundamental incompatibility, while a growth mindset treats friction as something a couple can work through together. The chapter on parents, teachers, and coaches is arguably the book's most consequential: Dweck's research shows that praising a child's intelligence ('you're so smart') reliably backfires, making children more fragile and failure-averse, while praising process and effort ('you found a strategy that worked') builds exactly the resilience adults are usually trying to instill.

Crucially, Dweck insists mindset is not itself a fixed trait. Nearly everyone carries both mindsets in different measure, the balance can vary by domain — a person might approach their career with real openness to growth while treating their marriage or their golf game with rigid, ego-protective fixedness — and the balance can be deliberately shifted with practice. The book's closing chapters offer a practical method for doing that: notice the specific situations that trigger a defensive, fixed-mindset reaction, learn to recognize the internal voice that shows up in those moments, and consciously substitute a growth-oriented response until it becomes closer to automatic. The payoff Dweck describes isn't becoming a different, permanently confident person — it's becoming someone whose relationship to difficulty changes enough that effort, setbacks, and unflattering feedback stop feeling like referendums on their worth.

sections.title: The Mindsets
sections.summary:
This opening section lays the foundation the rest of the book builds on: the split between a fixed mindset and a growth mindset, and the discovery that this split is not a minor personality quirk but a broad predictor of how people handle difficulty. Dweck opens with the question that drove her original research program — why do some people crumble after failure while others, facing the identical setback, seem to find it energizing rather than devastating? — and argues that the answer lies in what each group believes about whether ability itself can change.

The chapter's substance is the foundational research, particularly Dweck's early studies presenting children with puzzles of increasing difficulty. Children with a fixed mindset described a hard puzzle in the language of failure and self-doubt — some literally said things like 'I guess I'm not very smart' — and their performance on subsequent puzzles actually got worse. Children with a growth mindset responded to the same hard puzzle with visible enthusiasm, treating it as the most interesting one yet, and their performance held steady or improved. Dweck uses this asymmetry to define the two mindsets precisely: fixed-mindset thinking treats every task as a test of a permanent quality, while growth-mindset thinking treats it as a chance to develop a quality that is still in progress.

The section closes by previewing the shape of the whole book: since the fixed/growth split shows up this clearly in a controlled experiment with puzzles, Dweck argues it should also show up — and does — in how people handle real challenges in sports, work, relationships, and parenting, which is exactly the territory the following chapters cover.
keyLessons: Notice how you explain a setback to yourself — 'I'm just not good at this' points to a fixed mindset, 'I need a different strategy' points to a growth mindset.
Treat a hard task as information about where you are, not a verdict on what you're capable of becoming.
Watch actual behavior (which tasks someone picks, how they respond to a hard puzzle) rather than self-description — mindset shows up in choices, not just words.

sections.title: Inside the Mindsets
sections.summary:
Having established the two mindsets, this section digs into what 'success' and 'failure' actually mean inside each one, since Dweck argues people aren't just interpreting the same events differently — they're functionally playing different games with different scoring systems.

In the fixed mindset, success means proving you're smart or talented, and failure means the opposite has been proven — so the entire goal of any activity becomes validation rather than learning. In the growth mindset, success means stretching to learn something you didn't know before, so setbacks are simply part of the process rather than a verdict on it. This section also unpacks how effort itself gets read in opposite ways: in the fixed mindset, needing to work hard is itself faintly damning, since 'real' talent is supposed to make things look easy; in the growth mindset, effort is the very mechanism that turns raw ability into actual accomplishment, so working hard is a sign of engagement rather than a confession of weakness.

Dweck closes the section by connecting this to self-esteem: a self-image built on being validated as talented is brittle, because it depends on continuously winning, while a self-image built on the belief that you can develop is much harder to shake, because setbacks don't threaten the premise it rests on. This sets up the case studies in the following chapters, which are really extended illustrations of these two different scoring systems in action.
keyLessons: Ask what 'winning' actually means to you in a given pursuit — proving you already have it, or getting better at it.
Reframe needing to work hard at something as evidence you're engaged with it, not evidence you lack natural ability.
Build self-regard on your capacity to develop rather than on being validated as already good — it holds up better under setbacks.

sections.title: The Truth About Ability and Accomplishment
sections.summary:
This section takes aim directly at the 'natural talent' explanation for exceptional achievement, arguing that it is both scientifically weak and practically harmful, since it teaches people to wait for a gift instead of building the capacity themselves.

Dweck moves through case studies of people widely regarded as prodigies or naturals and shows, in each case, a long, often unglamorous history of sustained deliberate effort behind the results — years of practice, specific coaching, repeated failure, and course-correction that gets edited out of the retrospective 'natural talent' story once someone becomes famous. She argues that this editing is not neutral: it actively discourages other people from trying, because if greatness looks like something you're simply born with, effort looks pointless for anyone who wasn't.

The chapter concludes that a growth mindset is not just a nicer way to feel about setbacks — it's a more accurate model of how expertise actually gets built, and this accuracy is exactly what sustains the years of unglamorous effort that talent alone can't explain. This case-study approach is the bridge to the following two chapters, which apply the same argument specifically to sports and business.
keyLessons: Assume any impressive skill has an unglamorous effort history behind it, even when the public story only shows the finished result.
Don't use someone's early performance (or your own) as a ceiling — trajectory over time is a better predictor than starting point.
Treat 'talent' as a description of where someone started, not a claim about where they can end up.

sections.title: Sports: The Mindset of a Champion
sections.summary:
Dweck turns to sports specifically because athletic performance is unusually well-documented and commonly (and, she argues, wrongly) attributed almost entirely to natural physical gifts, making it a clean test case for the mindset framework.

The chapter profiles athletes and coaches who fall on both sides of the divide: competitors who treat every loss as a threat to their identity as a 'natural,' and become fragile or defensive as a result, versus competitors who treat losses as specific, fixable information and use them to train differently. Coaching philosophy gets similar treatment — Dweck highlights coaches who define success as full preparation and full effort rather than a flawless record, on the logic that a team held to the standard of effort can always meet it, while a team held to the standard of perfection eventually cannot.

The chapter closes by generalizing the lesson beyond sports: the athletes and coaches who sustain excellence over long careers are consistently the ones who never stopped treating themselves as works in progress, which is the same growth-mindset posture the book will go on to apply to business and parenting.
keyLessons: Define your own standard as full effort and preparation, not a flawless outcome — it's a standard you can actually meet every time.
Use a loss as a specific diagnostic (what exactly to adjust) rather than a global judgment (I'm not good enough).
Watch for identity-protecting behavior in competition — avoiding tougher opponents or making excuses in advance — as a fixed-mindset signal.

sections.title: Business: Mindset and Leadership
sections.summary:
This chapter applies the mindset framework to organizations, arguing that a leader's personal mindset doesn't stay personal — it sets the ceiling for how honestly an entire team or company can talk about its own problems.

Dweck profiles fixed-mindset executives who need to be visibly the smartest person in every room, who surround themselves with people unlikely to challenge them, and who treat bad news as a threat to be managed or suppressed rather than information to act on — a pattern she connects to some of the more dramatic corporate collapses of the era. Against this, she profiles growth-minded leaders who actively recruit people who might eventually outshine them, build feedback loops that surface problems early, and treat the organization as a vehicle for everyone's development rather than a stage for their own greatness.

The chapter's conclusion is that growth-mindset leadership is not simply a nicer management style — it's a structural advantage, because organizations that can hear bad news early and develop their people can keep adapting long after a founder's original insight has run its course.
keyLessons: Treat hiring people who might outshine you as a sign of strength, not a risk to be managed.
Build explicit channels for bad news to reach you early — a growth-mindset culture depends on people believing honesty won't be punished.
Judge leadership less by the leader's individual brilliance and more by whether the people around them are visibly developing.

sections.title: Relationships: Mindsets in Love (or Not)
sections.summary:
Dweck extends the framework into romantic relationships and friendships, arguing that the same fixed/growth split that shapes how people handle a hard exam or a business setback also shapes how they handle conflict with a partner.

In a fixed mindset, conflict or a partner's flaws get read as evidence of fundamental incompatibility — the underlying assumption is that a 'right' relationship should not require this much friction, so difficulty itself becomes proof of a mismatch. In a growth mindset, the same friction is simply what working through differences with another person actually looks like, and Dweck argues that couples who treat problems this way are far more likely to actually resolve them, because they're not simultaneously relitigating whether the relationship should exist at all. She also discusses how a fixed mindset shows up as score-keeping — cataloguing a partner's shortcomings as evidence in an ongoing case — versus a growth mindset's willingness to see a partner's behavior in context and as changeable.

The chapter closes by noting that this same distinction extends to friendships and to how people handle rejection more generally, reinforcing the book's broader claim that mindset is a single underlying orientation that shows up consistently across very different kinds of relationships.
keyLessons: Treat relationship friction as normal maintenance work, not proof that you chose the wrong partner.
Notice score-keeping (cataloguing a partner's flaws as an ongoing case) as a fixed-mindset habit that blocks resolution.
Extend the same growth-oriented reframing you'd use for a professional setback to conflict with people you're close to.

sections.title: Parents, Teachers, and Coaches: Where Do Mindsets Come From?
sections.summary:
This chapter is arguably the book's most practically consequential: Dweck's research shows that the specific language adults use with children — especially praise — is one of the most direct levers for shaping which mindset a child develops.

The central finding is counterintuitive: praising a child's intelligence or talent ('you're so smart') feels supportive in the moment but reliably backfires, making children more fragile, more failure-averse, and less willing to attempt harder tasks afterward, because it teaches them that their value is tied to a fixed quality that difficulty could disprove. Praising process instead — effort, strategy, persistence, improvement — produces the opposite effect, building children who seek out challenge because their sense of competence isn't riding on any single outcome. Dweck extends this beyond praise to labeling more broadly, arguing that even positive fixed labels like 'the smart one' or 'a natural' can quietly install a fixed mindset, and that the same dynamic applies to how teachers grade and how coaches give feedback, not just how parents compliment.

The chapter closes with the observation that adults often create fixed-mindset children with the best of intentions, simply by trying to make kids feel good in the moment rather than capable over time — which is exactly the trade-off the book asks parents, teachers, and coaches to reconsider.
keyLessons: Praise the specific process — effort, strategy, persistence — instead of a fixed trait like 'smart,' 'talented,' or 'a natural.'
Be cautious with positive labels too ('the smart one') — even flattering fixed labels can install fixed-mindset thinking.
When a child struggles, respond as a teacher diagnosing what to try next, not a judge delivering a verdict.

sections.title: Changing Mindsets
sections.summary:
The closing section shifts from diagnosis to practice, offering a concrete method for readers who recognize fixed-mindset patterns in themselves and want to shift toward a growth orientation.

Dweck's method starts with identifying personal fixed-mindset triggers — the specific situations, often involving criticism, comparison, or the risk of visible failure, that reliably provoke a defensive reaction. From there, she asks readers to notice and even name the internal 'fixed-mindset voice' that shows up in those moments — the inner narration that reframes a setback as a threat to your worth — so that it can be recognized as a voice rather than simply accepted as the truth. The final step is a conscious substitution: deliberately choosing and rehearsing a growth-oriented response until it becomes more automatic, the same way any other skill improves with repeated practice.

Dweck is careful to close without overpromising: she's explicit that mindset change is domain-specific, gradual, and never fully finished — most people retain some fixed-mindset triggers indefinitely — but she argues that even partial, deliberate movement toward a growth mindset changes how challenge, effort, and failure feel, which is the practical payoff the entire book has been building toward.
keyLessons: Identify your specific fixed-mindset triggers — the exact situations (harsh feedback, being outperformed, public failure) that provoke a defensive reaction.
Name your internal fixed-mindset voice so you can notice it and respond to it, rather than automatically believing it.
Expect mindset change to be gradual and domain-specific, not a single permanent switch you flip once.
Notice whether you're treating a challenge as a test of your worth (fixed mindset) or as an opportunity to develop (growth mindset).
Reframe effort as the mechanism of mastery, not evidence of low natural talent.
Seek out negative feedback deliberately — a growth mindset treats criticism as useful data, not a personal attack.
When praising others (especially children), praise process, strategy, and effort — not fixed traits like 'smart' or 'talented.'
Recognize that mindset varies by domain — you can have a growth mindset at work and a fixed one in relationships, so audit each area separately.
Treat setbacks and failure as information about what to try next, not as proof of a fixed identity or ceiling.
Notice your own 'fixed-mindset voice' in the moment (defensiveness, need to prove yourself) and consciously choose a growth-oriented response instead.
Build teams and relationships around growth — for leaders, that means creating a culture where mistakes are treated as learning, not liability.

quotes.text: The passion for stretching yourself and sticking to it, even (or especially) when it's not going well, is the hallmark of the growth mindset.

This growth mindset is based on the belief that your basic qualities are things you can cultivate through your efforts. Although people may differ in every which way—in their initial talents and aptitudes, interests, or temperaments—everyone can change and grow through application and experience.
Believing that your qualities are carved in stone—the fixed mindset—creates an urgency to prove yourself over and over.
When people with the fixed mindset opt for success over growth, what are they really trying to prove? That they're special. Even superior.
There were two meanings to ability, not one: a fixed ability that needs to be proven, and a changeable ability that can be developed through learning
the view you adopt for yourself profoundly affects the way you lead your life.
Becoming is better than being.
We like to think of our champions and idols as superheroes who were born different from us. We don't like to think of them as relatively ordinary people who made themselves extraordinary.
People may start with different temperaments and different aptitudes, but it is clear that experience, training, and personal effort take them the rest of the way.

Many of the most accomplished people of our era were considered by experts to have no future. Jackson Pollock, Marcel Proust, Elvis Presley, Ray Charles, Lucille Ball, and Charles Darwin were all thought to have little potential for their chosen fields.

Think about your hero. Do you think of this person as someone with extraordinary abilities who achieved with little effort? Now go find out the truth. Find out the tremendous effort that went into their accomplishment—and admire them more.

Many growth-minded people didn't even plan to go to the top. They got there as a result of doing what they love. It's ironic: The top is where the fixed-mindset people hunger to be, but it's where many growth-minded people arrive as a by-product of their enthusiasm for what they do.

In the fixed mindset, everything is about the outcome. If you fail—or if you're not the best—it's all been wasted. The growth mindset allows people to value what they're doing regardless of the outcome. They're tackling problems, charting new courses, working on important issues. Maybe they haven't found the cure for cancer, but the search was deeply meaningful.

In one world, failure is about having a setback. Getting a bad grade. Losing a tournament. Getting fired. Getting rejected. It means you're not smart or talented. In the other world, failure is about not growing. Not reaching for the things you value. It means you're not fulfilling your potential. In one world, effort is a bad thing. It, like failure, means you're not smart or talented. If you were, you wouldn't need effort. In the other world, effort is what makes you smart or talented.
Finding #2: Those with the growth mindset found setbacks motivating. They're informative. They're a wake-up call.
If you're somebody when you're successful, what are you when you're unsuccessful?

When people believe their basic qualities can be developed, failures may still hurt, but failures don't define them. And if abilities can be expanded—if change and growth are possible—then there are still many paths to success.

studies show that people are terrible at estimating their abilities. Recently, we set out to see who is most likely to do this. Sure, we found that people greatly misestimated their performance and their ability. But it was those with the fixed mindset who accounted for almost all the inaccuracy. The people with the growth mindset were amazingly accurate. When you think about it, this makes sense. If, like those with the growth mindset, you believe you can develop yourself, then you're open to accurate information about your current abilities, even if it's unflattering.

Is there something in your past that you think measured you? A test score? A dishonest or callous action? Being fired from a job? Being rejected? Focus on that thing. Feel all the emotions that go with it. Now put it in a growth-mindset perspective. Look honestly at your role in it, but understand that it doesn't define your intelligence or personality. Instead, ask: What did I (or can I) learn from that experience? How can I use it as a basis for growth? Carry that with you instead.
test scores and measures of achievement tell you where a student is, but they don't tell you where a student could end up.

After seven experiments with hundreds of children, we had some of the clearest findings I've ever seen: Praising children's intelligence harms their motivation and it harms their performance. How can that be? Don't children love to be praised? Yes, children love praise. And they especially love to be praised for their intelligence and talent. It really does give them a boost, a special glow—but only for the moment. The minute they hit a snag, their confidence goes out the window and their motivation hits rock bottom. If success means they're smart, then failure means they're dumb. That's the fixed mindset.

Parents think they can hand children permanent confidence—like a gift—by praising their brains and talent. It doesn't work, and in fact has the opposite effect. It makes children doubt themselves as soon as anything is hard or anything goes wrong. If parents want to give their children a gift, the best thing they can do is to teach their children to love challenges, be intrigued by mistakes, enjoy effort, and keep on learning. That way, their children don't have to be slaves of praise. They will have a lifelong way to build and repair their own confidence.

In fact, every word and action can send a message. It tells children—or students, or athletes—how to think about themselves. It can be a fixed-mindset message that says: You have permanent traits and I'm judging them. Or it can be a growth-mindset message that says: You are a developing person and I am interested in your development.
Don't judge. Teach. It's a learning process.

So what should we say when children complete a task—say, math problems—quickly and perfectly? Should we deny them the praise they have earned? Yes. When this happens, I say, "Whoops. I guess that was too easy. I apologize for wasting your time. Let's do something you can really learn from!"

As growth-minded leaders, they start with a belief in human potential and development—both their own and other people's. Instead of using the company as a vehicle for their greatness, they use it as an engine of growth—for themselves, the employees, and the company as a whole.

Instead, they are constantly trying to improve. They surround themselves with the most able people they can find, they look squarely at their own mistakes and deficiencies, and they ask frankly what skills they and the company will need in the future.

A no-effort relationship is a doomed relationship, not a great relationship. It takes work to communicate accurately and it takes work to expose and resolve conflicting hopes and beliefs. It doesn't mean there is no "they lived happily ever after," but it's more like "they worked happily ever after."

authorBio.name: Carol S. Dweck
authorBio.bio:
Carol Susan Dweck was born on October 17, 1946, and grew up in Brooklyn, New York, the middle child and only daughter of three. She has traced her early fascination with how people respond to being judged back to her sixth-grade classroom, where students were seated in IQ order and only the highest scorers were given classroom privileges — an experience she has said made her acutely aware of how much a single number can shape how a child sees their own potential. She graduated from Barnard College in 1967 and earned her PhD in psychology from Yale University in 1972.

Dweck built her academic career at the University of Illinois, Harvard, and Columbia before joining Stanford University in 2004, where she now holds the Lewis and Virginia Eaton Professorship of Psychology. Her research, beginning with a foundational 1988 paper on what she called 'implicit theories' of intelligence, established the fixed/growth mindset distinction as a serious line of experimental psychology years before Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2006) translated it for a general audience and turned it into one of the most widely cited ideas in education, parenting, and business writing.

Her mindset research has also drawn academic scrutiny: some researchers have reported difficulty replicating specific findings, and a large 2019 UK trial of a school-based mindset intervention found no measurable improvement in test scores, prompting ongoing debate about how directly the underlying theory translates into classroom interventions. Dweck has been elected to the National Academy of Sciences and was awarded the Yidan Prize for Education Research in 2017 for her contributions to the field.
notableWorks: Self-Theories: Their Role in Motivation, Personality, and Development

whoThisIsFor: Anyone stuck avoiding challenges out of fear of failure, and parents, teachers, or managers who want to understand how their feedback shapes other people's relationship to effort and ability.
whenToReadThis: Read when starting something difficult and unfamiliar, after a significant setback, or when giving regular feedback to children, students, or a team.
